sets.title: Equivalent ratios
sets.lead: Each box shows a ratio of filled (orange) to empty circles.
args: Shows 2 : 3 in its simplest form, using the fewest circles.
The only ratio built from more than 6 circles — it is 4 : 6, double of box A.
The only one where filled outnumber empty (3 : 2 — the ratio is "flipped").
The only ratio equivalent to 1 : 2 (twice as many empty as filled).
prompts: Which two boxes show the same ratio? How can you prove it?
If each ratio were a paint recipe, which would look the same color?

sets.title: Fraction · decimal · percent
sets.lead: Four ways to name a number — three are equal.
args: The only picture / model — 75 out of 100 squares shaded.
The only one written as a decimal (0.75).
A fraction that is not in lowest terms (6/8 = 3/4).
The odd one out — it equals 2/3, not 3/4.
prompts: Three of these are equal. Which is the impostor, and what could you change to make it match?
Which form would you rather use to compare with 0.8? Why?

sets.title: Unit rate — best buy

args: for 3 lb
for 2 lb
for 2 lb
for 5 lb

sets.lead: Four prices for the same item at different weights.
args: $2 per pound.
$2 per pound — the smallest amounts.
The only different unit price: $3 per pound (the worst deal).
$2 per pound — the only 5-pound (largest) amount.
prompts: Find the price per pound for each. Which is the best buy? The worst?
Three are the same deal in disguise. Which numbers made that hard to see?

sets.title: Comparing numbers & opposites

args: −5
|−5|

sets.lead: Four values to compare and order.
args: The only value less than zero — the opposite of 5.
The only positive whole number written plainly.
Written with absolute-value bars, but it still equals 5.
The only value between 0 and 1 — the only fraction, and the closest to zero.
prompts: Which two are equal? Which is farthest from zero? Which is closest?
Put all four in order from least to greatest.

sets.title: Exponents

args: 2<sup>3</sup>
3<sup>2</sup>
2·2·2

sets.lead: Evaluate each. Notice which ones are equal.
args: Exponent form that equals 8.
The only value that equals 9 — and the only odd result.
The only one written as repeated multiplication (expanded), but it equals 8.
The only one with no exponent, the smallest value, and equal to 2 × 3.
prompts: Which two are equal but written differently?
Is 2³ the same as 2 × 3? Convince the room.

sets.title: Equivalent expressions

args: x + x + 6

sets.lead: Which of these name the same value for every x?
args: The only factored form (uses parentheses) — equals 2x + 6.
The fully simplified standard form.
The impostor — it equals 2x + 3, not 2x + 6.
The only one that uses repeated addition (x + x).
prompts: Substitute x = 1 into each. Which one gives a different answer?
Three are equivalent. What is the same about them and different about the fourth?

sets.title: Coordinate plane & quadrants
sets.lead: Four points plotted on the coordinate plane.
args: The only point with both coordinates positive (Quadrant I).
The only point with a negative x and positive y (Quadrant II).
The only point where both coordinates are negative (Quadrant III).
The pattern-breaker: its y is −3, so it is NOT a mirror image of the others.
prompts: Three of these points are reflections of one another across the axes. Which one breaks the pattern?
How far apart are the two points that share an x-coordinate?

sets.title: One-step equations

args: x − 3 = 4

sets.lead: Solve each equation. Watch which solutions match.
args: The only addition equation whose solution is 7.
The only subtraction equation (x = 7).
The only multiplication equation (x = 7).
The impostor — its solution is 8, and it looks almost identical to box A.
prompts: Solve all four. Three share a solution — which is the odd one out?
Boxes A and D look nearly the same. What one change flips the answer?

sets.title: Inequalities on a number line
sets.lead: Each graph shows the solutions to an inequality.
args: Open circle at 3, arrow right: x > 3.
The only closed (filled) circle — it includes the boundary: x ≥ 3.
The only graph pointing left: x < 3.
The only one with a negative boundary: x > −3.
prompts: Which graphs include their boundary number? How can you tell?
Which two point the same direction? Which two start at the same number?

sets.title: Area of polygons
sets.lead: Find the area of each shape.
args: A rectangle with area 12 square units.
The only triangle — area = ½ · 8 · 3 = 12.
The only slanted shape (parallelogram) — area = 6 · 2 = 12.
The only square, and the only area that is NOT 12 (it is 16).
prompts: Find each area. Three match — which is different?
Which shape needs a "½" in its area rule? Why only that one?

sets.title: Volume of prisms
sets.lead: Find the volume of each rectangular prism.
args: The only cube (all edges equal) — volume 8.
A tall, thin box — volume 8.
The odd volume: 2 · 3 · 2 = 12.
A flat, wide box — volume 8.
prompts: Compute each volume. Which prism holds a different amount?
Three hold the same amount but look nothing alike. How is that possible?

sets.title: Describing data
sets.lead: Four dot plots of numerical data.
args: The only symmetric ("balanced") distribution, centered at 5.
The only one with no spread — every value is the same.
The only one with an outlier (10 sits far from the rest).
The only one with no repeats — evenly spaced and lopsided (skewed).
prompts: Which set has the most spread? Which has an outlier?
In which set would the mean and median be equal? Where would an outlier pull the mean?

sets.title: Is it a statistical question?

args: How tall are the students in our class?
How many pets does each student have?
How tall is our teacher?
How many minutes did students sleep last night?

sets.lead: A statistical question is one you expect to answer with data that VARIES.
args: A statistical question about height (inches) — answers vary from student to student.
A statistical question about a count of pets — answers vary.
The impostor — this has ONE answer (the teacher’s height), so it is not a statistical question.
A statistical question about time (minutes) — answers vary.
prompts: Which question would you answer with a single number instead of a graph? Why isn’t that "statistical"?
Reword box C so it becomes a statistical question.

sets.title: Which display fits?
sets.lead: Four ways to show data — but one shows something different.
args: A dot plot — shows every individual data value as a dot.
A histogram — groups the numbers into equal intervals; you can’t see each value.
A box plot — shows only five summary numbers (min, quartiles, median, max).
The impostor — a bar graph compares CATEGORIES, not numerical data (notice the gaps).
prompts: Three of these display numerical data; one compares categories. Which is different?
Which display shows the median at a glance? Which shows every single data point?

sets.title: Negative in real life

args: You owe a friend $5
5 feet below sea level
5 degrees below zero
You climb up 5 stairs

sets.lead: Each situation can be written with a positive or negative number.
args: Represents −5 — a debt (money).
Represents −5 — elevation below the surface.
Represents −5 — temperature below zero.
The impostor — this is +5 (going UP), the only gain / positive direction.
prompts: Three of these describe −5. Which one is positive? What does 0 mean in each situation?
What makes "up the stairs" different from the other three?

sets.title: Same ratio, different clothes

args: blue
red
2 blue to 5 red

sets.lead: Three of these show the SAME ratio in different forms.
args: A tape diagram showing 2 blue : 3 red.
A double number line showing 2 : 3 (and 4 : 6).
A ratio table for 2 : 3.
The impostor — this ratio is 2 : 5, not 2 : 3.
prompts: Three show the same ratio dressed up differently. Which one is a different ratio?
Which representation makes equivalent ratios easiest to see? Why?

sets.title: Match the phrase

args: n + n + n + 5

sets.lead: Which match the phrase "triple a number, then add 5"?
args: 3n + 5 — triple the number, then add 5. ✓
The impostor — 3(n + 5) adds 5 FIRST, then triples it (= 3n + 15).
n + n + n + 5 — "triple" as repeated addition, then add 5. ✓
5 + 3n — same as box A, just written in a different order. ✓
prompts: Which box does the "add 5" at the wrong time? What does it equal instead?
Substitute n = 2 into each. Which one is the odd result?

sets.title: Area vs perimeter
sets.lead: Compare these rectangles by area AND by perimeter.
args: Area 12, perimeter 16.
Area 12, but the smallest perimeter (14).
The odd AREA — the only square and the only area that isn’t 12 (area 16). Yet its perimeter (16) matches box A!
Area 12, but a huge perimeter (26) — long and skinny.
prompts: Sort by area — which is different? Now sort by perimeter — does a different one stand out?
Which two rectangles have the same perimeter but different area?
